title: Saudi Aramco Halts Crude Supplies to India as Pipeline Shutdown Bites
excerpt: With the East-West pipeline down, the kingdom's state oil company has told Indian refiners no term crude is coming — forcing expensive spot-market replacements.
body:
• Saudi Aramco has told Indian refiners it will not supply crude until further notice, according to The Economic Times, after the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
  • Aramco, which has supplied about 9% of India's crude imports since the war began, has halted shipments through both the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz.
  • Indian refiners can secure replacement barrels on the spot market, but at higher cost: Brent surged to around $108 a barrel on Wednesday, and tanker freight rates have risen.
  • Saudi Arabia has sold some spot cargoes that could reach India through Hormuz, but access and pricing remain uncertain.

India's refineries are facing a sudden supply shock from their most reliable supplier. Saudi Aramco, the kingdom's state oil company, has told Indian refiners they will not receive crude supplies until further notice, according to The Economic Times, citing people familiar with the matter.

The halt follows the shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which moves crude from the kingdom's eastern fields to its Red Sea export terminals. With the pipeline down, Aramco has stopped all supplies to India through both the Red Sea and the Strait of Hormuz, the report said.

Why it hurts

Saudi crude is not a marginal input for India. Aramco has supplied roughly 9% of India's crude imports since the beginning of the conflict — a share built on annual term contracts that give refiners volume certainty and stable pricing. Aramco typically does not sell in the spot market, so losing term barrels means replacing them in the open market.

The timing is punishing. Brent crude surged to around $108 a barrel on Wednesday and remains above $105, while tanker freight rates have climbed as few shipowners dare to enter the Strait of Hormuz or the Red Sea to load from Saudi's two main export ports. The discounts that once made Russian crude a cheap substitute have narrowed or disappeared.

A wider Gulf disruption

The pipeline shutdown is part of a broader disruption to Gulf energy flows. The Houthis declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia on July 20, and have since claimed attacks on Saudi-linked tankers, Yanbu oil facilities and the Jazan refinery on the Red Sea coast. Earlier in the year, Aramco was already handling Asian crude allocations on an ad hoc basis, with some Indian refiners told their full allocations were conditional on securing vessels.

Saudi Arabia has sold some spot cargoes to traders expected to deliver small volumes to Indian refiners through Hormuz. But spot purchases offer neither the certainty nor the pricing advantage of term supplies, and Saudi crude shipments to Asia — 4.9 million barrels a day last year — are closely watched as a barometer of regional demand.

What comes next

Indian refiners have diversified before: they have pulled in barrels from Brazil, Guyana, Norway and the United States when Gulf supplies tightened. But Middle Eastern grades suit their refinery configurations best, and every substitute comes with longer voyages, higher freight and price risk.

For Indian consumers, the question is how long the pipeline stays shut. If "until further notice" stretches into weeks, replacement costs will feed through to import bills and, eventually, pump prices — at a moment when crude is already above $105.

nri_angle: Higher crude costs feed directly into India's import bill and fuel prices, squeezing the remittance value and household budgets of NRIs tied to the Indian economy.
